# serde_yaml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_yaml/^0.9/

## Expand description

Rust library for using the [Serde](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde) serialization framework with data in
[YAML](https://yaml.org/) file format. *(This project is no longer maintained.)*

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::collections::BTreeMap;
fn main() -> Result<(), serde_yaml::Error> {
    // You have some type.
    let mut map = BTreeMap::new();
    map.insert("x".to_string(), 1.0);
    map.insert("y".to_string(), 2.0);
    // Serialize it to a YAML string.
    let yaml = serde_yaml::to_string(&map)?;
    assert_eq!(yaml, "x: 1.0\ny: 2.0\n");
    // Deserialize it back to a Rust type.
    let deserialized_map: BTreeMap<String, f64> = serde_yaml::from_str(&yaml)?;
    assert_eq!(map, deserialized_map);
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-serde-derive)Using Serde derive

It can also be used with Serde’s derive macros to handle structs and enums defined in your program.

Structs serialize in the obvious way:

```
use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, PartialEq, Debug)]
struct Point {
    x: f64,
    y: f64,
}
fn main() -> Result<(), serde_yaml::Error> {
    let point = Point { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 };
    let yaml = serde_yaml::to_string(&point)?;
    assert_eq!(yaml, "x: 1.0\ny: 2.0\n");
    let deserialized_point: Point = serde_yaml::from_str(&yaml)?;
    assert_eq!(point, deserialized_point);
    Ok(())
}
```
Enums serialize using YAML’s `!tag` syntax to identify the variant name.

```
use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, PartialEq, Debug)]
enum Enum {
    Unit,
    Newtype(usize),
    Tuple(usize, usize, usize),
    Struct { x: f64, y: f64 },
}
fn main() -> Result<(), serde_yaml::Error> {
    let yaml = "
        - !Newtype 1
        - !Tuple [0, 0, 0]
        - !Struct {x: 1.0, y: 2.0}
    ";
    let values: Vec<Enum> = serde_yaml::from_str(yaml).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(values[0], Enum::Newtype(1));
    assert_eq!(values[1], Enum::Tuple(0, 0, 0));
    assert_eq!(values[2], Enum::Struct { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 });
    // The last two in YAML's block style instead:
    let yaml = "
        - !Tuple
          - 0
          - 0
          - 0
        - !Struct
          x: 1.0
          y: 2.0
    ";
    let values: Vec<Enum> = serde_yaml::from_str(yaml).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(values[0], Enum::Tuple(0, 0, 0));
    assert_eq!(values[1], Enum::Struct { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 });
    // Variants with no data can be written using !Tag or just the string name.
    let yaml = "
        - Unit  # serialization produces this one
        - !Unit
    ";
    let values: Vec<Enum> = serde_yaml::from_str(yaml).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(values[0], Enum::Unit);
    assert_eq!(values[1], Enum::Unit);
    Ok(())
}
```

# tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/^3/

## Expand description

This is a library for creating temporary files and directories that are automatically deleted when no longer referenced (i.e., on drop).

- Use `tempfile()``std::fs::File`
- Use `NamedTempFile::new()`*named*temporary file that can be referred to its path.
- Use `tempdir()`
- Use `spooled_tempfile()`

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

This crate provides several approaches to creating temporary files and directories.
[ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) relies on the OS to remove the temporary file once the last handle is closed.

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`[both rely on Rust destructors for cleanup.](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

`tempfile` will (almost) never fail to cleanup temporary resources. However `TempDir` and
`NamedTempFile` will fail if their destructors don’t run. This is because `tempfile` relies on
the OS to cleanup the underlying file, while `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on rust
destructors to do so. Destructors may fail to run if the process exits through an unhandled
signal interrupt (like `SIGINT`), or if the instance is declared statically (like with
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/issues/62)), among other possible reasons.

[§](https://docs.rs#unexpected-file-deletion)Unexpected File Deletion

Most operating systems periodically clean up temporary files that haven’t been accessed recently
(often on the order of multiple days). This issue does not affect unnamed temporary files but
can invalidate the paths associated with named temporary files on Unix-like systems because the
temporary file can be unlinked from the filesystem while still open and in-use. See the
[temporary file cleaner](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners) section for more security implications.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This section discusses security issues relevant to Unix-like operating systems that use shared temporary directories by default. Importantly, it’s not relevant for Windows or macOS as both operating systems use private per-user temporary directories by default.

Applications can mitigate the issues described below by using [ env::override_temp_dir](https://docs.rs/env/fn.override_temp_dir.html) to
change the default temporary directory but should do so if and only if default the temporary
directory (

[) is unsuitable (is world readable, world writable, managed by a temporary file cleaner, etc.).](https://docs.rs/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`env::temp_dir`[§](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners)Temporary File Cleaners

In the presence of pathological temporary file cleaner, relying on file paths is unsafe because a temporary file cleaner could delete the temporary file which an attacker could then replace.

This isn’t an issue for [ tempfile](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) as it doesn’t rely on file paths. However,

[and temporary directories](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`*do*rely on file paths for

*some*operations. See the security documentation on the

[and the](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[types for more information.](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`Mitigation:

- This is rarely an issue for short-lived files as temporary file cleaners usually only remove temporary files that haven’t been modified or accessed within many (10-30) days.
- Very long lived temporary files should be placed in directories not managed by temporary file cleaners.

[§](https://docs.rs#access-permissions)Access Permissions

Temporary *files* created with this library are private by default on all operating systems.
However, temporary *directories* are created with the default permissions and will therefore be
world-readable by default unless the user has changed their umask and/or default temporary
directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#denial-of-service)Denial of Service

If the file-name randomness ([ Builder::rand_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.rand_bytes)) is too small and/or this crate is built
without the

`getrandom` feature, it may be possible for an attacker to predict the random file
names chosen by this library, preventing temporary file creation by creating temporary files
with these predicted file names. By default, this library mitigates this denial of service
attack by:- Defaulting to 6 random characters per temporary file forcing an attacker to create billions of files before random collisions are expected (at which point you probably have larger problems).
- Re-seeding the random filename generator from system randomness after 3 failed attempts to
create temporary a file (when the `getrandom`feature is enabled as it is by default on all major platforms).

[§](https://docs.rs#early-drop-pitfall)Early drop pitfall

Because `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on their destructors for cleanup, this can lead
to an unexpected early removal of the directory/file, usually when working with APIs which are
generic over `AsRef<Path>`. Consider the following example:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::process::Command;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let temp_dir = tempdir()?;
// Spawn the `touch` command inside the temporary directory and collect the exit status
// Note that `temp_dir` is **not** moved into `current_dir`, but passed as a reference
let exit_status = Command::new("touch").arg("tmp").current_dir(&temp_dir).status()?;
assert!(exit_status.success());
```
This works because a reference to `temp_dir` is passed to `current_dir`, resulting in the
destructor of `temp_dir` being run after the `Command` has finished execution. Moving the
`TempDir` into the `current_dir` call would result in the `TempDir` being converted into
an internal representation, with the original value being dropped and the directory thus
being deleted, before the command can be executed.

The `touch` command would fail with an `No such file or directory` error.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a temporary file and write some data into it:

```
use tempfile::tempfile;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file = tempfile()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```
Create a named temporary file and open an independent file handle:

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
use std::io::{Write, Read};
let text = "Brian was here. Briefly.";
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file1 = NamedTempFile::new()?;
// Re-open it.
let mut file2 = file1.reopen()?;
// Write some test data to the first handle.
file1.write_all(text.as_bytes())?;
// Read the test data using the second handle.
let mut buf = String::new();
file2.read_to_string(&mut buf)?;
assert_eq!(buf, text);
```
Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let dir = tempdir()?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```

# ma_zscheme_yaml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ma-zscheme-yaml/0.1.0/target-redirect/ma_zscheme_yaml/

## Expand description

YAML/file-backed [ DotRegistry](https://docs.rs/ma-zscheme/0.1.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/ma_zscheme/registry/trait.DotRegistry.html) for ma-zscheme.

`SchemeConfig` stores dot-path key-value pairs in a YAML file under
`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/ma/zscheme-data.yaml`.  It is the default persistent
backend for the `zscheme` CLI.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use ma_zscheme_yaml::SchemeConfig;
use ma_zscheme::DotRegistry;
let path = SchemeConfig::default_path().unwrap();
let mut cfg = SchemeConfig::load(&path);
cfg.set("my.aliases.sky", "did:ma:abc");
cfg.save(&path).unwrap();
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Scheme](https://docs.rs/struct.SchemeConfig.html)- Config
- Flat key-value configuration store backed by a YAML file.

---

[203](#203)        assert!(cfg.get_str("my.aliases.sky").is_none());
[204](#204)        assert!(cfg.get_str("my.aliases.ms").is_none());
[205](#205)        assert_eq!(cfg.get_str("my.i18n"), Some("nb".into())); }
[207](#207)
[208](#208)    #[test]
[209](#209)    fn delete_exact_leaf() {
[210](#210)        let mut cfg = SchemeConfig::new();
[211](#211)        cfg.set("my.i18n", "nb");
[212](#212)        DotRegistry::delete_subtree(&mut cfg, ".my.i18n");
[213](#213)        assert!(cfg.get_str("my.i18n").is_none());
[214](#214)    }
[215](#215)
[216](#216)    #[test]
[217](#217)    fn delete_absent_is_noop() {
[218](#218)        let mut cfg = SchemeConfig::new();
[219](#219)        cfg.set("my.i18n", "nb");
[220](#220)        DotRegistry::delete_subtree(&mut cfg, "my.nonexistent");
[221](#221)        assert_eq!(cfg.get_str("my.i18n"), Some("nb".into()));
[222](#222)    }
[223](#223)
[224](#224)    #[test]
[227](#227)    fn list_sorted_with_leading_dot() {
[228](#228)        let mut cfg = SchemeConfig::new();
[229](#229)        cfg.set("my.aliases.z", "did:ma:z");
[230](#230)        cfg.set("my.aliases.a", "did:ma:a");
[231](#231)        let pairs = DotRegistry::list(&cfg, "my.aliases");
[232](#232)        assert_eq!(pairs.len(), 2);
[233](#233)        assert_eq!(pairs[0].0, ".my.aliases.a");
[234](#234)        assert_eq!(pairs[1].0, ".my.aliases.z");

[300](#300)        let path = dir.path().join("test.yaml");
[301](#301)
[302](#302)        let mut cfg = SchemeConfig::new();
[303](#303)        cfg.set("my.aliases.sky", "did:ma:abc");
[304](#304)        cfg.set("my.i18n", "nb");

}## Expand description

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Return the value stored at `path`, or `None` if absent.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/ma_zscheme/registry.rs.html#68-70)#### fn [is_read_only](https://docs.rs#method.is_read_only)(&self, _path: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/ma_zscheme/registry.rs.html#68-70)

#### fn [is_read_only](https://docs.rs#method.is_read_only)(&self, _path: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Whether this path is read-only (writes and deletes should be rejected).

Default: all paths are writable. Override in stores that protect
certain keys (e.g. `EgoConfig` protects `.my.identity.*`).

Resolve an actor target such as `@alias#fragment` or
`did:ma:…#fragment` to a full DID+fragment string.

This provided implementation delegates to
[ resolve_alias](https://docs.rs/trait.DotRegistry.html#method.resolve_alias); you normally do not need to
override it.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Returns `Err` if the alias is unknown or the target is malformed.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# SchemeConfig in ma_zscheme_yaml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ma-zscheme-yaml/0.1.0/ma_zscheme_yaml/struct.SchemeConfig.html

`pub struct SchemeConfig { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Flat key-value configuration store backed by a YAML file.

Keys are stored without a leading `.` (e.g. `"my.aliases.sky"`).

# eclectica 0.9.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/eclectica/0.9.2/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# ma-zscheme-ipfs 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ma-zscheme-ipfs/0.1.0

IPFS-backed [`DotRegistry`] for ma-zscheme.

# Status

This crate is a skeleton. Implementations are stubbed with `todo!()`.

A future implementation will store dot-path values as IPFS DAG-CBOR objects, enabling fully decentralised, content-addressed configuration. Changes will be published to IPNS so the registry survives across sessions without a local file.

---

# IpfsRegistry in ma_zscheme_ipfs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ma-zscheme-ipfs/0.1.0/ma_zscheme_ipfs/struct.IpfsRegistry.html

`pub struct IpfsRegistry { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

IPFS-backed registry.

Values are fetched from and stored to IPFS via Kubo or a gateway.
The in-memory `cache` holds values for the current session.

[§](https://docs.rs#not-yet-implemented)Not yet implemented

All mutating methods currently `todo!()`.

# ma-zscheme 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ma-zscheme/0.1.0

ma-zscheme — Scheme evaluator for the ma actor network.

## Overview

Provides a complete Scheme evaluator with:

- Proper tail-call optimisation (TCO) via an explicit `'tco`loop
- Named `let`(`let loop …`)
- `apply`as a first-class procedure
- ma-specific primitives: dot-paths (`.my.path`), actor calls (`@alias`/`did:ma:…`), and CID loading (`<bafy…>`)
- Pipe threading (`val | (f arg) | g`)

## Usage

Implement [`SchemeCtx`] for your host context, then call [`eval_source`]:

```
use ma_zscheme::{eval_source, init_session_env, SchemeCtx, Ctx};
let ctx: Ctx = Rc::new(MyCtx::new());
init_session_env();
let result = eval_source("(+ 1 2)", ctx).await?;
```

---

# futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3/

## Expand description

Abstractions for asynchronous programming.

This crate provides a number of core abstractions for writing asynchronous code:

- [Futures](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)are single eventual values produced by asynchronous computations. Some programming languages (e.g. JavaScript) call this concept “promise”.
- [Streams](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)represent a series of values produced asynchronously.
- [Sinks](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html)provide support for asynchronous writing of data.
- [Executors](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)are responsible for running asynchronous tasks.

The crate also contains abstractions for [asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) and
[cross-task communication](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html).

Underlying all of this is the *task system*, which is a form of lightweight
threading. Large asynchronous computations are built up using futures,
streams and sinks, and then spawned as independent tasks that are run to
completion, but *do not block* the thread running them.

The following example describes how the task system context is built and used within macros and keywords such as async and await!.

```
fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new().expect("Failed to build pool");
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::unbounded::<i32>();
    // Create a future by an async block, where async is responsible for an
    // implementation of Future. At this point no executor has been provided
    // to this future, so it will not be running.
    let fut_values = async {
        // Create another async block, again where the Future implementation
        // is generated by async. Since this is inside of a parent async block,
        // it will be provided with the executor of the parent block when the parent
        // block is executed.
        //
        // This executor chaining is done by Future::poll whose second argument
        // is a std::task::Context. This represents our executor, and the Future
        // implemented by this async block can be polled using the parent async
        // block's executor.
        let fut_tx_result = async move {
            (0..100).for_each(|v| {
                tx.unbounded_send(v).expect("Failed to send");
            })
        };
        // Use the provided thread pool to spawn the generated future
        // responsible for transmission
        pool.spawn_ok(fut_tx_result);
        let fut_values = rx
            .map(|v| v * 2)
            .collect();
        // Use the executor provided to this async block to wait for the
        // future to complete.
        fut_values.await
    };
    // Actually execute the above future, which will invoke Future::poll and
    // subsequently chain appropriate Future::poll and methods needing executors
    // to drive all futures. Eventually fut_values will be driven to completion.
    let values: Vec<i32> = executor::block_on(fut_values);
    println!("Values={:?}", values);
}
```
The majority of examples and code snippets in this crate assume that they are inside an async block as written above.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, returning a tuple of all results once complete.
- [pending](https://docs.rs/macro.pending.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which yields to the event loop once.
- [pin_mut](https://docs.rs/macro.pin_mut.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/macro.poll.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which returns the result of polling a future once within the
current `async`context.
- [ready](https://docs.rs/macro.ready.html)
- Extracts the successful type of `Poll<T>`.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `async-await`and- `std`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. If multiple futures are ready,
one will be pseudo-randomly selected at runtime. Futures directly
passed to `select!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/macro.select_biased.html)- biased - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. Unlike `select!``select_biased!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/macro.stream_select.html)- select - `async-await`and- `std`
- Combines several streams, all producing the same `Item`type, into one stream. This is similar to`select_all`but does not require the streams to all be the same type. It also keeps the streams inline, and does not require`Box<dyn Stream>`s to be allocated. Streams passed to this macro must be`Unpin`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, resolving to a `Result`

- `DotRegistry`— pluggable backing store for dot-path config.
- [value](https://docs.rs/value/index.html)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [eval_](https://docs.rs/fn.eval_source.html)- source
- Evaluate all top-level Scheme expressions in `source`in the session environment and return the value of the last expression.
- [get_env](https://docs.rs/fn.get_env.html)
- Return the current session environment, creating one lazily if needed.
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_session_env.html)- session_ - env
- Initialise a fresh session environment (call on login / script start).
- [reset_](https://docs.rs/fn.reset_session_env.html)- session_ - env
- Clear the session environment (call on logout / script end).

# lib.rs - source

# ma_zscheme/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! ma-zscheme — Scheme evaluator for the ma actor network.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! ## Overview
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! Provides a complete Scheme evaluator with:
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! - Proper tail-call optimisation (TCO) via an explicit `'tco` loop
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! - Named `let` (`let loop …`)
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! - `apply` as a first-class procedure
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! - ma-specific primitives: dot-paths (`.my.path`), actor calls (`@alias`
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!   / `did:ma:…`), and CID loading (`<bafy…>`)
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! - Pipe threading (`val | (f arg) | g`)
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! ## Usage
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! Implement [`SchemeCtx`] for your host context, then call [`eval_source`]:
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! ```ignore
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! use ma_zscheme::{eval_source, init_session_env, SchemeCtx, Ctx};
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! let ctx: Ctx = Rc::new(MyCtx::new());
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! init_session_env();
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! let result = eval_source("(+ 1 2)", ctx).await?;
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! ```
[24](https://docs.rs#24)
[25](https://docs.rs#25)pub mod dot;
[26](https://docs.rs#26)pub mod eval;
[27](https://docs.rs#27)pub mod host;

[56](https://docs.rs#56)/// Return the current session environment, creating one lazily if needed.

[58](https://docs.rs#58)/// # Panics
[59](https://docs.rs#59)///
[60](https://docs.rs#60)/// Panics if the thread-local `SESSION_ENV` has already been destroyed
[61](https://docs.rs#61)/// (i.e., during thread shutdown after `reset_session_env` was not called).
[62](https://docs.rs#62)#[must_use]
[63](https://docs.rs#63)pub fn get_env() -> Env {
[64](https://docs.rs#64)    SESSION_ENV.with(|e| {
[65](https://docs.rs#65)        let mut inner = e.borrow_mut();
[66](https://docs.rs#66)        if inner.is_none() {
[67](https://docs.rs#67)            *inner = Some(Env::new_root());
[68](https://docs.rs#68)        }
[69](https://docs.rs#69)        inner.as_ref().unwrap().clone()
[70](https://docs.rs#70)    })
[71](https://docs.rs#71)}
[72](https://docs.rs#72)

Host interface threaded through every recursive eval call.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Evaluate a ma dot-path command and return the result as a `SchemeVal`.

Handles get (`.my.path`), set (`.my.path: value`),
delete (`.my.path:`), and meta-verbs (`.my.path!verb args`).

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Returns `Err` if the dot-path command is invalid or the host refuses it.

# parse_actor_command in ma_zscheme::dot - Rust

```
pub fn parse_actor_command(
    cmd: &
```
[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    registry: &dyn [DotRegistry](https://docs.rs/registry/trait.DotRegistry.html),

Parse an actor command string into `(target_with_fragment, verb, args)`.

Accepted forms:

- `@alias#fragment:verb arg1 arg2`
- `@alias#fragment`
- `@alias:verb arg1`
- `did:ma:abc#fragment:verb arg1`

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Returns `Err` if the alias is unknown in `registry`.

# parse_dot_command in ma_zscheme::dot - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ma-zscheme/0.1.0/ma_zscheme/dot/fn.parse_dot_command.html

## Expand description

Parse a dot-path command string into `(path, DotOp)`.

Formats:

- `.my.path`→- `Get`
- `.my.path: value`→- `Set("value")`
- `.my.path:`→- `Delete`
- `.my.path!verb args`→- `Meta { verb, args }`

Returns `None` if the input is empty after stripping the leading `.`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use ma_zscheme::{parse_dot_command, DotOp};
let (path, op) = parse_dot_command(".my.i18n: nb").unwrap();
assert_eq!(path, "my.i18n");
assert!(matches!(op, DotOp::Set(v) if v == "nb"));
let (path, op) = parse_dot_command(".my.aliases.sky").unwrap();
assert_eq!(path, "my.aliases.sky");
assert!(matches!(op, DotOp::Get));
```

---

## Expand description

The operation encoded in a dot-path command string.

`.my.path` — return the stored value or list children.

`.my.path: value` — store `value` at the path.

`.my.path:` — delete the subtree rooted at the path.

`.my.path!verb [args]` — dispatch a side-effect verb.

Performs copy-assignment from

`source`.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html#method.clone_from)

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.Borrow.html#tymethod.borrow)

Mutably borrows from an owned value.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/borrow/trait.BorrowMut.html#tymethod.borrow_mut)

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`clone_to_uninit`)

`self` to

`dest`.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Return the value stored at `path`, or `None` if absent.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/ma_zscheme/registry.rs.html#68-70)#### fn [is_read_only](https://docs.rs#method.is_read_only)(&self, _path: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/ma_zscheme/registry.rs.html#68-70)

#### fn [is_read_only](https://docs.rs#method.is_read_only)(&self, _path: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Whether this path is read-only (writes and deletes should be rejected).

Default: all paths are writable. Override in stores that protect
certain keys (e.g. `EgoConfig` protects `.my.identity.*`).

Resolve an actor target such as `@alias#fragment` or
`did:ma:…#fragment` to a full DID+fragment string.

This provided implementation delegates to
[ resolve_alias](https://docs.rs/trait.DotRegistry.html#method.resolve_alias); you normally do not need to
override it.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Returns `Err` if the alias is unknown or the target is malformed.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

Simple in-memory registry backed by a `HashMap`.

This is the default when no file or external store is configured.
Data is **not** persisted across process restarts.

# ma_zscheme::dot - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ma-zscheme/0.1.0/ma_zscheme/dot/index.html

## Expand description

Dot-command parsing utilities.

`DotOp` and the associated parse functions are the canonical way to
interpret dot-path commands.  They are shared across all `SchemeCtx`
implementations so any host can call them without re-implementing the
grammar.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [DotOp](https://docs.rs/enum.DotOp.html)
- The operation encoded in a dot-path command string.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_link_value.html)- link_ - value
- Returns `true`if the string looks like an IPFS CID or`did:ma:`link.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_actor_command.html)- actor_ - command
- Parse an actor command string into `(target_with_fragment, verb, args)`.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_dot_command.html)- dot_ - command
- Parse a dot-path command string into `(path, DotOp)`.

---

# ma_zscheme::eval - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ma-zscheme/0.1.0/ma_zscheme/eval/index.html

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [eval](https://docs.rs/fn.eval.html)
- Evaluate a parsed `SchemeExpr`.
- [eval_](https://docs.rs/fn.eval_str.html)- str
- Evaluate a Scheme source string.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_link_value.html)- link_ - value
- True if `s`looks like an IPFS CID or a`did:ma:`DID. Used to decide whether a`<token>`or``include``path should be fetched.

# ma_zscheme::registry - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ma-zscheme/0.1.0/ma_zscheme/registry/index.html

## Expand description

`DotRegistry` — pluggable backing store for dot-path config.

Implement this trait to connect any key-value store (flat file, IPFS,
database, or an in-memory map) to the evaluator.  The evaluator never
touches storage directly; all access goes through
[ SchemeCtx::eval_dot](https://docs.rs/host/trait.SchemeCtx.html#tymethod.eval_dot), which delegates CRUD
to whatever registry the host provides.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use ma_zscheme::registry::{DotRegistry, InMemoryRegistry};
let mut reg = InMemoryRegistry::default();
reg.set("my.aliases.sky", "did:ma:abc");
assert_eq!(reg.resolve_alias("sky"), Some("did:ma:abc".to_string()));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#extension-points)Extension points

The trait has two provided methods with sensible defaults:

- `is_read_only`- `EgoConfig`protects- `.my.identity.*`).
- `resolve_target`- `my.aliases.<name>`convention.

Future registry implementations may include an IPFS-backed store
(e.g. `IpfsRegistry`) or a database-backed store.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [InMemory](https://docs.rs/struct.InMemoryRegistry.html)- Registry
- Simple in-memory registry backed by a `HashMap`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [DotRegistry](https://docs.rs/trait.DotRegistry.html)
- Pluggable dot-path key-value store.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [normalize_](https://docs.rs/fn.normalize_key.html)- key
- Strip leading `.`from a dot-path key for normalised internal storage.

---

# car-validator 0.32.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/car-validator/0.32.0

# car-validator

Precondition checking and action validation for the [Common Agent Runtime](https://github.com/Parslee-ai/car).

## What it does

Validates actions against runtime state and registered tool schemas before execution.
Checks preconditions (eq, neq, gt, lt, gte, lte, exists, not_exists, contains), verifies
required tool parameters, and confirms state dependencies are present. Returns structured
`ValidationResult` with all errors.

## Usage

```
use ;
use StateStore;
let state = new;
let result = validate_action;
if !result.valid
```
Part of [CAR](https://github.com/Parslee-ai/car) -- see the main repo for full documentation.

---
